title: Laboratory frictional stability data from borehole core from the Horn River Basin, Canada, 2018-2024
abstract: This data set is comprised of experimental data collected from frictional stability tests in the laboratory to characterise both the frictional strength (µ) and the frictional stability (a-b) of lithologies acquired from the Horn River Basin, Canada. We prepared test specimens from core samples, collected at various depths from wells drilled through varying stratigraphies and subjected them to in situ pressure conditions before shearing. See Horn_River-Sampling_Test_Information accompanying data file for depth, location and specific test condition information. The triaxial experimental apparatus, used to undertake the friction tests, was designed and constructed at the University of Liverpool (Faulkner and Armitage, 2013). This apparatus is capable of triaxial deformation under confining pressures up to 250 MPa, applied using silicon oil confining medium, pore fluid pressures up to 200 MPa and differential loads up to 300 kN. These systems are all servo-controlled, with the confining and pore fluid pressure controlled and measured to a resolution <0.1 mm3. The servo-controlled pore fluid system can also be used as a volumometer, allowing the monitoring of changes in pore volume to a resolution of <0.1 mm3. De-ionised water was used as the pore fluid in this study, and was held at a constant 10 MPa in all tests. title: Experimental protocols used in tactile perception of materials: a mini review
abstract: Tactile perception plays a central role in how humans evaluate and interact with materials, influencing perceived roughness, softness, friction, warmth, wetness, comfort, quality, and usability. In recent years, experimental studies on tactile perception have expanded across diverse material systems, including textiles, synthetic fibers, plastics, wood, building materials, soft rubbers, textured surfaces, and haptic overlays. However, the experimental protocols used across these studies remain highly varied. This mini-review examines recent experimental approaches adopted in tactile perception studies of materials, with emphasis on work published within approximately the last 5 years. We identified common methodological strategies, including psychophysical rating scales, forced-choice and pairwise-comparison tasks, tactile-only and visual–tactile testing, active-touch standardization, instrumented material characterization, and multisensory or haptic-interface protocols. By comparing these approaches, the review highlights how differences in material selection, sensory access, exploratory movement, subjective rating methods, and physical characterization influence the interpretation of tactile perception data. We also discuss key research gaps, including the need for standardized reporting, cross-material benchmark datasets, diverse participant populations, improved control of touch behavior, and stronger links between tactile perception experiments and material-design guidel

title: Incorporation of Graphene-based Materials in Modern Powder-based Processes
abstract: The incorporation of graphene-based materials into powder-based manufacturing processes offers opportunities to tailor material processing and performance. However, achieving controlled graphene characteristics, retaining its functionality during manufacturing, and developing scalable incorporation methods remain important challenges. This thesis investigates these aspects through graphene oxide (GO) deposition on metallic powders, the retention and tribological performance of graphene-based materials in thermal spraying, and the influence of GO on the laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB) processing of pure copper.A molecular-level mixing method was developed to deposit GO onto metallic powder particles using APTES as a coupling agent. Adjusting the APTES concentration and GO loading enabled control over coating characteristics and surface coverage. By adapting the mixing conditions and chemical parameters, the methodology was scaled from 20 to 500 g batches that were repeatedly used to produce 10 kg of GO-coated copper powder.Graphene retention and tribological functionality were investigated in Al₂O₃ coatings containing graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs), produced by suspension plasma spraying, and GO-containing WC–Co–Cr coatings, produced by high-velocity air-fuel spraying. Graphene-based materials were retained after deposition in both systems but underwent progressive structural and chemical modification during sliding wear. title: ADDITIVE MANUFACTURING OF FUELS AND PROPELLANTS: MULTI-MATERIAL INTERFACES AND INTERPENETRATING POLYMER NETWORKS
abstract: In the field of propulsion, additive manufacturing (AM) can enable the construction of solid fuel and propellant grains with complex geometries and multiple formulations, which provide greater control over thrust. However, the traditional polymeric binder for fuels and propellants, hydroxyl-terminated polybutadiene (HTPB), is poorly suited for AM due to its slow curing. While photocurable and photo-thermal dual-cure polymers (e.g., acrylates) allow for rapid polymerization, they come with the drawbacks of inferior combustion and mechanical properties. Additionally, the interfaces caused by AM and the functional grading of formulations significantly affect the grain’s mechanical properties. The mechanical properties are also affected by the processing conditions and part design, including the spatial variance in degree of cure, bulk porosity, and stress concentrations within the geometry of the grain.Limited studies exist on the mechanical properties of additively manufactured solid propellants and other highly loaded particle-reinforced composites, so the first study of this dissertation used multi-formulation photocurable particle-reinforced composites with glass microspheres as surrogate materials that were made via casting and vibration assisted printing to test the effects of the processing conditions, part design, manufacturing methods, and material changes on the tensile and density properties for two different material formulations. title: COMPREHENSIVE ANALYSIS OF THE OPERATIONAL PERFORMANCE OF BRAKE SHOES FOR PASSENGER RAILWAY VEHICLES

publisher: Ukrainian State University of Railway Transport
abstract: The paper addresses the problem of improving the efficiency of railway rolling stock braking systems through a comprehensive analysis of the design, tribological, thermal, operational, and economic characteristics of modern brake blocks. The performance of the braking system is largely determined by the frictional properties of brake blocks, which directly affect braking efficiency, braking distance, wheel wear, maintenance costs, and the overall operational safety of railway vehicles. The increasing axle loads, higher train speeds, and more demanding operating conditions require the development and application of friction materials capable of maintaining stable braking performance under a wide range of service conditions.A comparative analysis of cast iron, high-phosphorus cast iron, composite, and sintered metal brake blocks was carried out. Their structural features, frictional properties, thermal behavior, durability, advantages, disadvantages, and fields of practical application were evaluated. Particular attention was paid to the comparison of traditional cast iron brake blocks with modern composite brake blocks, which have become widely used in freight and passenger rolling stock due to their improved wear resistance, lower weight, and higher friction coefficient.A comprehensive approach for evaluating the operational efficiency of railway brake blocks is proposed. title: The Buy-in Effect: When Increasing Initial Effort Encourages Follow-Through
publisher: Institute for Operations Research and the Management Sciences
abstract: Behavioral interventions often focus on reducing friction to encourage behavior change. In contrast, we provide evidence that adding initial friction to a sign-up process can increase follow-through behavior. In a field experiment with a state department of transportation ([Formula: see text]), we test whether adding modest friction during sign-up for a carpool platform increases usage. Although a more effortful sign-up process leads to 25% fewer sign-ups, overall usage increases. Importantly, these results were only partly explained by selection: Using an intent-to-treat analysis, participants with a more effortful sign-up process took 1.6 times more carpool trips per week over four months, leading to more overall trips despite fewer users. In a second experiment with online task work, participants with more effortful sign-up were 37% more likely to return the next day and completed more work overall. These results suggest that adding friction may be an overlooked strategy when follow-through, rather than initial uptake, is the primary goal. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral economics and decision analysis. title: Dynamics of Coacervate Gels
abstract: Polyelectrolytes are ubiquitous in nature and play a fundamental role in many biological and synthetic systems. Hydrogels, as soft materials composed of crosslinked polymer networks, exhibit unique mechanical properties that make them widely applicable in diverse fields. In this dissertation, I investigate the properties of coacervate gels formed by combining linear polyelectrolyte chains with a crosslinked hydrogel network. First, the structural and mechanical properties of the coacervate gels are systematically characterized using a range of experimental techniques and compared with those of the native hydrogel. At low salt concentrations, the addition of the guest polymer leads to gel shrinkage, an increase in shear modulus and diffusion coefficient, and a decrease in the friction coefficient. In contrast, these effects become much less pronounced at high salt concentrations due to electrostatic screening. Next, the dynamics of the guest polymer within the hydrogel matrix are examined. The polymer exhibits a distinct diffusive–subdiffusive–diffusive behavior across different time scales, which differs significantly from its behavior in bulk solution. Finally, several future research directions are proposed, including variations in key experimental parameters and development of methods to extract the kinetic constants associated with the guest–host interactions. title: Cyclical Force Generation for Triboelectric Nanogenerators: A Review of Mechatronic Approaches, Challenges and Future Perspectives
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert low-frequency and irregular mechanical energy into electrical energy for self-powered sensors, wearable electronics, Internet-of-Things devices and distributed energy systems. Although major advances have been made in triboelectric materials, surface engineering and device architectures, the mechanical excitation applied during TENG testing remains an important source of experimental variability. Manual tapping, pressing and sliding can introduce uncontrolled changes in force, displacement, velocity, frequency, contact area and waveform, making comparison between experiments difficult. This review examines cyclical force generation as a controllable subsystem for TENG characterization. Linear actuators, servo systems, electrodynamic shakers, cam-follower and crank-slider mechanisms, electromechanical testing machines and tribometers are compared in terms of force/displacement control, frequency, repeatability, cost and suitability. The review also summarizes the mechanical parameters that should be measured together with electrical output and presents a conceptual closed-loop cyclical force generator (CFG) incorporating an actuator, force sensor, displacement sensor, controller, driver, data-acquisition system and TENG fixture. title: Current-driven Magnetic Skyrmions for Encoding/Storing Information: Manipulation and Dynamics in Nanoscale Structures
abstract: This dissertation investigates the dynamics of current-driven magnetic skyrmions, topological solitons in magnetic materials with broken spatial inversion symmetry, for low-power spintronic applications like racetrack memory and multilevel data storage. Skyrmions’ small size and low driving current requirements make them promising information carriers. The research examines skyrmion motion under driving currents, pinning effects, and thermal fluctuations, using numerical simulations (Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation), analytical studies (Thiele equation), and theoretical modeling to design novel data storage devices. The study analyzes skyrmion motion amidst pinning potentials from material imperfections. Simulations reveal that thermal fluctuations vary with damping: acting as a frictional force at low damping or a driving force aiding depinning at high damping. The Thiele equation quantifies this, though its accuracy wanes at low temperatures with pinning. The skyrmion Hall angle, influenced by current and pinning, provides insights for ambient-condition devices. These findings underpin a proposed multilevel data storage device, where controlled current positions skyrmions at pinning sites for high-density, low-power encoding. The research also explores altermagnetic (ATM) skyrmions, which exhibit d-wave symmetry via exchange-driven spin splitting. title: Dynamic Performance of Waste Astragalus gummifer Bark-Reinforced Polymer Composites: Effect of Resin and Filler Ratio
abstract: In this study, the effects of resin type (epoxy and unsaturated polyester) and reinforcement ratio (40–70 wt%) on the dynamic behavior of waste Astragalus bark (Astragalus gummifer – AG)-reinforced polymer composites were experimentally investigated. AGE (epoxy matrix) and AGP (polyester matrix) specimen groups, fabricated by mechanical mixing and curing under 25 bar pressure, were subjected to modal analysis using the free vibration method, and their natural frequency and damping characteristics were determined. The findings demonstrate that epoxy-matrix systems exhibit higher stiffness, producing higher natural frequencies than the AGP group across all configurations; the highest frequency was recorded at 16.78 Hz in the AGE1 specimen containing 40 wt% AG. Increasing the reinforcement ratio systematically reduced the natural frequency in both groups by increasing system mass. In terms of damping capacity, the polyester matrix showed a distinct advantage over epoxy due to its viscoelastic character; the damping ratio of the AGP4 specimen containing 70 wt% AG (10.31%) was approximately 3.36 times that of its counterpart AGE4 specimen (3.07%). Increasing the AG reinforcement ratio triggered interfacial friction mechanisms, elevating the damping ratio in both matrix systems. title: Instability of natural convection in a vertical flat porous microchannel
journal: International Journal of Numerical Methods for Heat &amp Fluid Flow
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to focus on the hydrodynamic stability of steady-state natural convection inside a vertical flat porous microchannel. The main objective is to investigate the transition conditions from stable to unstable flow under the Boussinesq approximation, explicitly incorporating velocity slip and temperature jump boundary conditions at the channel walls. Design/methodology/approach For the first time for this specific channel geometry, the small perturbation method is applied to derive a modified Orr–Sommerfeld equation that accounts for microscale effects and porous media properties. The resulting eigenvalue problem is solved numerically to determine the neutral stability thresholds and analyze the comprehensive effects of the Knudsen, Darcy and Prandtl numbers on the flow behavior. Findings Critical Grashof numbers, where the imaginary part of the eigenvalues changes sign, were successfully determined. The slip effect acts as a stabilizing factor because reduced fluid-wall interaction lowers friction, requiring a higher temperature difference to destabilize the flow. Conversely, increasing the Darcy number reduces the critical Grashof number toward an asymptotic constant, as less porous material intensifies flow velocity and disturbances due to decreased internal pressure. title: Enhancing cyclic charging-discharging performance of a latent heat storage unit using tree-shaped fins: Effects of fractal level and bifurcation angle on heat transfer and entropy generation
journal: International Communications in Heat and Mass Transfer
abstract: The low thermal conductivity of organic phase change materials limits the latent heat thermal energy storage performance. Most studies on tree-shaped fins examine melting or solidification separately, while this study numerically investigates the heat transfer and entropy generation characteristics of lauric acid during a consecutive melting–solidification process. Compared with rectangular fins, tree-shaped fins reduce the melting time, solidification time, and total process time by up to 45.81%, 47.23%, and 46.79%, respectively, and increase the energy storage power and energy release power by up to 84.58% and 90.22%, respectively. Relative to the one-level fractal cases, increasing the fractal level respectively reduces the melting time and solidification time by up to 21.21% and 28.74%, and respectively increases the energy storage power and energy release power by up to 27.07% and 43.58%. Furthermore, increasing the bifurcation angle from 30° respectively reduces the melting time and solidification time by up to 40.00% and 43.08%, and respectively increases the energy storage power and energy release power by up to 66.60% and 78.54%. Heat transfer entropy generation dominates the total entropy generation. title: Building a Self-Improving Agentic Harness for RSE Projects
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AI coding agents have moved from curiosities to capable collaborators in only a few years [4,5]. Early evidence was mixed [2,5], and as late as 2025 studies showed limited success on real software tasks that varied by domain and developer experience [1]. Over the period we report on (November 2025 – August 2026), both models and practice improved: orchestrator-driven multi-agent workflows [19], repeated adversarial review [6,7], context engineering, MCP tool calling, and project-specific skills (stored, version-controlled prompts invoked by name) [12,13]. Practice, discipline, and tooling separate agentic engineering from "vibe coding" [18]; adoption ranges from prohibition to treating the harness as shared infrastructure [3], and industry teams now build "software factories" [20,21,22]. This poster presents a semi-autonomous, self-improving, spec-driven [10,11], end-to-end development lifecycle, agentic software factory initially prototyped within the HyperShell project [14,15,16]; composed of eight agent skills plus wiki as context. Each feature moves through a fixed sequence (shape, plan, build, blind adversarial review, publish) and leaves a dated design record in the repository. We then ported the factory to a second research code, xdu, a parallel file-metadata indexer for HPC file systems, to test whether the method transfers. title: Color Changes in Natural Diamonds During Cutting and Polishing: The Role of Crystal Defects, Plastic Deformation, and Technological Factors
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Author: Nona D. Dronova Article type: Research-based scientific article derived from a 1991 Candidate of Sciences dissertation Fields: Mineralogy, Crystallography, Gemology, Diamond Processing Technology Abstract This article presents a systematic analysis of the mechanisms responsible for changes in the coloration of natural diamonds during their transformation into polished gemstones. The study examines the relationships between the initial optical properties of rough diamonds, crystal lattice defects, nitrogen-related color centers, plastic deformation, and the mechanical and thermal conditions of diamond processing. The research summarized here combines statistical investigations of diamond color before and after processing with optical spectroscopy, photoluminescence measurements, structural defect analysis, and experimental modeling of diamond–tool interactions. Particular attention is devoted to nitrogen-related N3 centers, dislocation structures, internal stresses, and localized plastic deformation as factors influencing the optical behavior of diamond crystals. The results indicate that diamond color may change during mechanical processing and that such changes are associated with the interaction of intrinsic crystal characteristics and processing-induced structural modifications. title: Regenerative braking control for electric vehicles with battery and safety constraints
abstract: Regenerative braking recovers energy while slowing an electric vehicle. Its contribution is limited by battery charge acceptance, motor capability, and tire grip. When the battery charging limit falls, friction braking may need to replace the lost regenerative torque. Different actuator response times can then cause a shortfall in total braking torque. This mini-review examines how battery limits and brake control are coordinated. It compares rule-based, fuzzy, predictive, and learning-based methods, with attention to actuator response and validation. It also examines dual-motor torque allocation and one-pedal control, using documented production functions as examples. Immediate battery protection is distinguished from long-term battery aging. The reviewed studies show why lower charging current alone does not establish a battery-life benefit. A key control task is to manage changes in regenerative capability during braking. Predicting these changes may help prepare the friction brakes, but the current battery and tire limits must still be respected. The review proposes combined battery and road test cases. It also defines torque-deficit measures for assessing brake transitions. Future studies should report recovered energy alongside deceleration, wheel slip, actuator delay, and battery response under matched test conditions.

title: Hybrid Sliding-Mode-Based Wheel Slip Control for Brake-by-Wire Vehicles with In-Wheel Motors
abstract: Sliding-mode control (SMC) is valued in automotive applications for its robustness and its low computational cost, although chattering remains a practical obstacle. Higher-order and adaptive formulations reduce chattering, but each carries limitations that may restrict their use in wheel slip control. This paper presents a hybrid low-level controller that combines a first-order sliding-mode (FOSM) term with a proportional–integral (PI) term acting on the same slip error. The two branches are weighted by a hyperbolic tangent function, so that the FOSM term governs the response towards the reference slip and the PI term governs it within a narrow band around the reference. Because the weighting is continuous, the transfer between branches introduces no step change in the torque demand. The controller is embedded in a three-level brake-by-wire architecture with series brake blending between in-wheel motors and friction brakes. The study uses an experimentally validated 14-DOF vehicle model and proposes a benchmarking procedure for comparison against a velocity-scheduled PI baseline. The results suggest improved slip tracking of the braking manoeuvre.

title: A Data Analysis and Comparison of Traditional and Alternative Powertrains in Motorsport
abstract: Motorsport has depended on internal combustion engines (ICEs) for decades, but growing concerns about energy efficiency and environmental impact have increased interest in alternative powertrain technologies. This paper compares internal combustion engine (ICE), battery-electric vehicle (BEV), and hydrogen fuel-cell electric vehicle (FCEV) powertrains in motorsport. The three powertrains are evaluated according to well-to-wheels and powertrain efficiency, energy replenishment, environmental impact, economic factors, and regulatory development. Published data are collected and analyzed to quantify well-to-wheels energy consumption, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, and thermodynamic efficiency, with comparisons also made between motorsport and conventional vehicles to examine how the distinct performance requirements of motorsport affect powertrain efficiency and environmental impact. For the selected racing cases, BEVs and FCEVs exhibit approximately 42.4% and 47.6% of the WTW energy consumption of ICEs, respectively, while their estimated WTW GHG emissions are 21.5% and 3.25% of those of ICEs under the selected upstream energy pathways. The analysis shows that ICEs offer well-proven high-performance characteristics and fast refueling, but they have a lower energy-conversion efficiency and produce direct GHG emissions.
